PullRequest.Title: Automations: graduate settings
PullRequest.Body:
Cloud Automations now defaults to enabled. Both Automations settings are graduated out of Experimental and Advanced.

Tested with the Automations contribution tests and verified in Settings with no user overrides.

Findings.ConfidenceRationale: The setting-to-refresh call path is direct and unconditional for a non-enterprise default GitHub account: the changed default feeds `enabled`, the autorun creates the store, and then awaits `refresh()`. The repository code explicitly enumerates the filesystem and network operations and their limits. Only prevalence and real-world repository/automation counts are uncertain; the mechanism is not.
Findings.PerformanceResource: Filesystem stats/reads, shared-process IPC calls, GitHub API requests, and hydrated definition/history objects.
Findings.PerformanceScaling: Per window launch, filesystem discovery grows with up to 10 recent workspaces times up to 50 parent lookups. Network work grows with effective repository count R and definition count D: at least capability/list calls per eligible repository, one detail hydration per definition, and one history request per definition, with active-run detail requests on top. Repository refresh is serialized; definition hydration is five-wide and history is four-wide.
Findings.PerformanceOutcome: Excessive background filesystem and network I/O after workbench restoration, with avoidable resource contention and bandwidth use.
Findings.PreviousBehavior: With the prior default `false`, users who had not opted in failed the `enabled` gate, no `GitHubCloudAutomationStore` was created, and startup/restoration caused zero cloud-automation filesystem or API work.
Findings.ChangedBehavior: Users without an explicit override now automatically create the cloud store and run a full catalogue-and-history refresh after every workbench restoration, even if they never open or invoke Automations.
Findings.CausalDiffEvidence: The added `default: true` at `automations.contribution.ts:41` changes the no-override value consumed by `CloudAutomationStore.enabled`; that value makes its autorun create `GitHubCloudAutomationStore` and immediately call `this.refresh()` after the default sessions provider is registered post-restore. With the prior `default: false`, the same autorun left `store` undefined and made no requests, as also codified by the existing `default-off ... create no API requests` test.
Findings.Title: Defer the default-on cloud refresh until Automations is used
Findings.Impact: A signed-in GitHub.com user can incur dozens to hundreds of filesystem, shared-process IPC, and GitHub API operations after opening a window without using Automations, consuming bandwidth/battery and contending with normal post-startup work. The cost is especially visible for users with several recent repositories or many cloud definitions.
Findings.Evidence: `CopilotChatSessionsProvider` is constructed at `WorkbenchPhase.AfterRestored` and always constructs `CloudAutomationStore` for the default provider. When enabled, `CloudAutomationStore` immediately calls `refresh()`, which invokes `refreshRepositories` and then `refreshHistory`. `refreshRepositories` serially resolves up to 10 Agents recent workspaces; each local resolution can perform up to 50 parent `.git` stats plus config reads. It then performs `getConfiguration` and a paginated definition list for every discovered/persisted repository, hydrates every definition in batches of five, and `refreshHistory` performs one `listRuns` per definition (plus detail calls for active runs) with concurrency four. Definitions are only memory-cached, so this repeats on each new workbench process/window.
Findings.Recommendation: Keep the graduated setting on, but defer store refresh and recent-workspace discovery until the Automations UI/tool first requests cloud data (coalescing that first load), or otherwise restrict the automatic post-restore path to a cheap persisted signal and schedule any necessary refresh as background work.

Scenarios.Scenario: Open or restore a workbench window while signed in to a GitHub.com default account without an explicit cloud-automation setting override.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The provider is created at `WorkbenchPhase.AfterRestored`; its async refresh is not awaited by contribution registration, so it is off the direct startup-blocking path. It nevertheless begins immediately after restore and competes with post-startup work for filesystem, IPC, network, CPU, and allocation resources.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Discovers GitHub repositories by walking parents and reading Git configuration.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Up to 10 Agents-owned recent workspaces per launch, each with up to 50 parent-directory `.git` stat probes plus `.git`/config reads; workspaces are processed serially.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: With the cloud setting default false and no user/experiment override, the enabled gate prevented store creation and these launch-time probes did not occur.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Off the direct startup blocker but part of the automatic post-restore refresh and must finish before the cloud catalogue becomes ready.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Acquires a GitHub account API client through shared-process IPC and fetches repository capabilities, automation catalogues/details, and run history.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: For effective repository count R, one capability request per repository and one paginated list (up to 10 pages) per eligible repository; for D returned definitions, one detail request and one history request per definition, plus detail requests for active tasks. Repository processing is serial, detail hydration five-wide, and history four-wide.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Absent an explicit opt-in, the prior false default caused zero cloud-automation IPC/API requests. The PR makes this boundary automatic for eligible signed-in users.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The catalogue and history cannot become ready until these calls finish; they are asynchronous and off direct workbench startup, but consume shared-process/network capacity during post-restore.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Loads and updates account-scoped known repository references in profile machine storage.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Reads the account repository set during refresh and reads/writes it once again when persisting eligible repositories.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The storage methods existed, but the default-off path did not invoke them after restoration for users without an override.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Synchronous profile-storage work occurs inside repository refresh but is small relative to filesystem and network fan-out.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Effective discovered/persisted GitHub repository count R (including up to 10 Agents recents), automation definition count D across eligible repositories, and active task count within up to 50 recent runs per definition.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Recent-workspace Git resolution and repository refresh are sequential. All store operations are serialized by a `Sequencer`; definition details are fetched in batches of five per repository, and history requests use a global limiter of four. Thus requests are bounded but can form a prolonged burst rather than an unbounded simultaneous fan-out.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Each new workbench process starts with empty in-memory definition/history caches. Repository identities persist in profile storage, but definitions and history do not, so the full refresh repeats per window/process. Client acquisition is cached for the store lifetime; concurrent definition refreshes are coalesced by `refreshPromise`, history refreshes by `historyRefresh`, and repository/definition data then remains warm in memory until another explicit refresh, account/client change, or disposal. There is no cross-process positive cache for definitions/history.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High: the changed default directly controls the observable gate; repository code proves immediate store construction and refresh, and existing tests prove the old disabled gate made no API calls.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The exact share of users with a non-enterprise default GitHub account, the number of Agents recents/persisted repositories, server response times, and automation counts are unknown. The repository permits 10 recents and up to 1,000 listed summaries per repository, so realistic multi-repository users still incur material work even though worst-case sizes are uncertain.
Scenarios.Verdict: Reportable: the default flip eagerly adds a scaling filesystem/IPC/network refresh after every restoration for users who may never use Automations. The work is not startup-blocking, which limits severity, but the background resource cost and diff causality are concrete.

Scenarios.Scenario: Open the Automations UI or invoke an automation tool after restoration.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Rendering or invoking an Automations surface requires provider catalogue state; an in-flight cold refresh can delay cloud results, while a completed eager refresh makes first use faster. Explicit mutations and tool/trigger loads remain user-initiated critical-path network work.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Reads cloud automation catalogue/history and lazily loads tool/trigger catalogues.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Cold first use reaches the same R-repository and D-definition GitHub request set; warm first use performs no catalogue/history boundary calls unless it explicitly refreshes. Loading tools or triggers adds one separately cached API call each when requested.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Explicitly opted-in users already had this first-use behavior. For users with no override, cloud automation was unavailable and issued no calls; the reported regression is the work being moved before any first use, not the existing on-demand boundaries.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Cold network work blocks cloud catalogue availability; warm cached data is immediate. Tool/trigger calls block only the corresponding requested configuration.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Repository and definition counts on cold load; one tool catalogue and one trigger catalogue request on their respective first uses.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Cold catalogue refresh uses the same serialized repository processing, five-wide detail hydration, and four-wide history limiter. Subsequent refresh requests coalesce while in flight; mutation operations serialize through the store sequencer.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: If the automatic post-restore refresh completed, first use is warm from in-memory catalogue/history caches. If it is still running, refresh promises coalesce duplicate reads. Tools/triggers remain separately lazy and cache successful results for the account lifetime; failed loads can retry. A new process loses catalogue/history warmth.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High for cache/coalescing behavior from `refreshPromise`, `historyRefresh`, and account-lifetime tool/trigger caches.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The first-use latency benefit from prefetching depends on whether the user opens Automations and how quickly after restoration. No measurement establishes that this benefit outweighs eager cost for the broader default-on population.
Scenarios.Verdict: No separate finding: first-use request fan-out is pre-existing for enabled users and is coalesced/bounded. This scenario supports deferring the newly eager refresh until actual use while preserving behavior.

Scenarios.Scenario: Browse or search Settings for the graduated Automations settings.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Configuration registration happens during module contribution loading; the changed metadata does not add work beyond existing property registration.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: No asynchronous or repeated changed work.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Configuration metadata is registered once; Settings indexing/search uses the existing configuration registry. Removing tags changes categorization only and creates no new cache state or invalidation loop.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: None material for performance; this is metadata-only.
Scenarios.Verdict: No performance issue: removing `experimental` and `advanced` tags and updating tests do not change expensive work, frequency, scale, or lifetime.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over both changed files and traced the default change through provider construction, cache ownership, filesystem discovery, shared-process/network calls, cardinality, and concurrency. Submitted one medium-severity eager-work finding for the automatic default-on post-restore cloud refresh; tag/test changes have no performance effect.

Stats.CostNote: Copilot SDK reports nano-AI units and model billing multipliers; it does not provide a USD conversion.
